title: Cohesion and Adhesion in Liquids: Surface Tension and Capillary Action
lead: The molecules of a liquid attract one another, and they attract the molecules of whatever the liquid touches. This section names the two kinds of attraction, cohesive forces within a liquid and adhesive forces between a liquid and its surroundings, and follows what they do: the surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched sheet that can hold up an insect or a needle, the gas inside a bubble is squeezed to a pressure that grows as the bubble shrinks, the lining of the lungs uses the same effect to help you breathe out, a drop meets a solid at a contact angle that says which of the two forces is winning, and a liquid climbs or is pushed down in a narrow tube by a height that follows from its surface tension, its density and the radius of the tube.
summary_html:
• Attractive forces between molecules of the same type are called cohesive forces.
  • Attractive forces between molecules of different types are called adhesive forces.
  • Cohesive forces between molecules cause the surface of a liquid to contract to the smallest possible surface area. This general effect is called surface tension.
  • Capillary action is the tendency of a fluid to be raised or suppressed in a narrow tube, or capillary tube which is due to the relative strength of cohesive and adhesive forces.
notes: The seven problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out: the surface tension of an alveolus’s fluid, the force on a 3.50 cm slide wire in ethyl alcohol, the height sap rises in a xylem tube, the effective surface tension of a rubber balloon, water in paraffin and silver tubes, the two soap bubbles that merge, and the ratio of the heights of ethyl alcohol and water; so is the unkeyed problem of 11.9 on the device that reaches a negative pressure of 25.0 atm.

Problems 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 have no keyed answer and are left out: the surface tension of the fluid lining an alveolus, the force on a 3.50 cm slide wire in ethyl alcohol, the height sap rises in a xylem tube, the effective surface tension of a rubber balloon, water raised in paraffin and silver tubes, the two soap bubbles that merge into one, and the ratio of the heights to which ethyl alcohol and water are raised. They are not floating; rather, they are supported by the surface of the liquid. (a) An insect leg dents the water surface. F_ST is a restoring force (surface tension) parallel to the surface. (b) An iron needle similarly dents a water surface until the restoring force (surface tension) grows to equal its weight.

The force needed to hold the wire in place is F = γL = γ(2l), since there are two liquid surfaces attached to the wire. This force remains nearly constant as the film is stretched, until the film approaches its breaking point.

With the valve closed, two balloons of different sizes are attached to each end of a tube. Upon opening the valve, the smaller balloon decreases in size with the air moving to fill the larger balloon. The pressure in a spherical balloon is inversely proportional to its radius, so that the smaller balloon has a greater internal pressure than the larger balloon, resulting in this flow.

Surface tension as a function of surface area. The surface tension for lung surfactant decreases with decreasing area. This ensures that small alveoli don’t collapse and large alveoli are not able to over expand.

In the photograph, water beads on the waxed car paint and flattens on the unwaxed paint. (a) Water forms beads on the waxed surface because the cohesive forces responsible for surface tension are larger than the adhesive forces, which tend to flatten the drop. (b) Water beads on bare paint are flattened considerably because the adhesive forces between water and paint are strong, overcoming surface tension. The contact angle θ is directly related to the relative strengths of the cohesive and adhesive forces. The larger θ is, the larger the ratio of cohesive to adhesive forces. (credit: P. P. Urone)

(a) Mercury is suppressed in a glass tube because its contact angle is greater than 90°. Surface tension exerts a downward force as it flattens the mercury, suppressing it in the tube. The dashed line shows the shape the mercury surface would have without the flattening effect of surface tension. (b) Water is raised in a glass tube because its contact angle is nearly 0°. Surface tension therefore exerts an upward force when it flattens the surface to reduce its area. — (a) Capillary action depends on the radius of a tube. The smaller the tube, the greater the height reached. The height is negligible for large-radius tubes. (b) A denser fluid in the same tube rises to a smaller height, all other factors being the same.

exercises.prompt: Is surface tension due to cohesive or adhesive forces, or both?

answer.solution: Surface tension is due to cohesive forces alone. The molecules of a liquid attract one another, and a molecule at the surface has neighbors on one side only, so it is pulled inward toward the body of the liquid. The result is that the surface contracts to the smallest area it can and behaves like a stretched sheet, which is what surface tension is. Adhesive forces act between the liquid and something else, such as a solid it touches, and they decide the contact angle and capillary action rather than the tension of the surface itself.

exercises.prompt: Is capillary action due to cohesive or adhesive forces, or both?

answer.solution: Both. Adhesive forces between the liquid and the wall of the tube set the contact angle, and so decide whether the liquid is raised or suppressed and which way the meniscus curves. Cohesive forces give the liquid its surface tension, and it is the surface tension pulling along the curved surface at the wall that lifts or pushes down the column; a liquid with no surface tension would not climb however well it wet the glass. The height $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$ carries both, the surface tension $\kgamma$ from cohesion and the contact angle $\theta$ from the balance of adhesion against cohesion.

exercises.prompt: Birds such as ducks, geese, and swans have greater densities than water, yet they are able to sit on its surface. Explain this ability, noting that water does not wet their feathers and that they cannot sit on soapy water.

answer.solution: A bird that is denser than water cannot float in the ordinary sense, any more than the iron needle can; what holds it up is the surface. Because water does not wet the feathers, the contact angle is large and the water does not soak in, so the feathers trap air and present a great length of unwetted surface to the water. The surface of the water dents under the bird and its restoring force, surface tension, acts along the whole of that contact line, and its upward parts add up to the bird’s weight, just as $\kwgt = \kgamma L\sin\theta$ holds the insect up. Soap lowers the surface tension of water to about half, and it also wets the feathers, so the length of dry surface and the pull per unit length both fall; the surface can no longer carry the weight, water soaks into the plumage, and the bird sinks lower and gets wet.

exercises.prompt: Water beads up on an oily sunbather, but not on her neighbor, whose skin is not oiled. Explain in terms of cohesive and adhesive forces.

answer.solution: The cohesive forces within the water are the same in both cases, so the difference lies in the adhesive forces between the water and the skin. Oil is like the wax on a car: the adhesive forces between water and oil are weak, so cohesion wins, the contact angle is large, and the water draws itself up into beads that touch the skin along a small area. Bare skin is more like bare paint: the adhesive forces between water and skin are strong enough to compete with cohesion, so the contact angle is small and the drops are flattened and spread out into a film.

exercises.prompt: Could capillary action be used to move fluids in a “weightless” environment, such as in an orbiting space probe?

answer.solution: Yes, and better than on Earth. Capillary action comes from the pull of surface tension along the wall of a tube, which has nothing to do with gravity; what limits the height on Earth is the weight of the column, which is why $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$ has $\kg$ in its denominator. In an orbiting probe the fluid and the tube are both in free fall, so nothing balances the pull of the surface, and a wetting fluid drawn into a tube keeps going along it. The text notes that capillary action can move liquids horizontally over very large distances on Earth for the same reason. Spacecraft do use wetting surfaces, narrow channels and screens to gather and move propellants and water where there is no “down” to help.

exercises.prompt: What effect does capillary action have on the reading of a manometer with uniform diameter? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: None, if the two arms of the manometer have the same diameter and hold the same fluid. Capillary action raises or suppresses the fluid in each arm by the same height $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$, because $\kgamma$, $\theta$, $\krho$ and $r$ are the same on both sides, and a manometer reads the difference in level between its two arms, so the two capillary shifts cancel. If the arms differed in diameter the shifts would differ, and the reading would be off by the difference between them, which is one reason manometer tubes are made alike and not too narrow.

exercises.prompt: Pressure between the inside chest wall and the outside of the lungs normally remains negative. Explain how pressure inside the lungs can become positive (to cause exhalation) without muscle action.

answer.solution: The alveoli are lined with fluid and behave like hundreds of millions of tiny bubbles. Surface tension in the lining of each one pulls it inward and raises the pressure of the air inside it by $\kPr = 4\kgamma/r$, just as it does for a soap bubble. When the muscles that hold the chest expanded relax, nothing opposes that pull, so the alveoli contract, the air in them is squeezed to a pressure above the pressure outside the body, and it flows out. That is why exhaling is passive and why, as the text says, surface tension will expel air from the lungs even when there is paralysis; the negative pressure between the chest wall and the lungs is what keeps them inflated against this pull between breaths.

exercises.prompt: What is the pressure inside an alveolus having a radius of $2.50\times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$ if the surface tension of the fluid-lined wall is the same as for soapy water? You may assume the pressure is the same as that created by a spherical bubble.

answer.hint: Treat the alveolus as a spherical bubble, so that $\kPr = 4\kgamma/r$, and take the surface tension of soapy water from Table 11.3.

exercises.prompt: What is the gauge pressure in millimeters of mercury inside a soap bubble 0.100 m in diameter?

answer.hint: The bubble is given by its diameter, and $\kPr = 4\kgamma/r$ wants its radius. Convert the pascals to mm Hg with 1.00 mm Hg = 133 N/m², as Example 11.11 does.

exercises.prompt: Figure 11.32(a) shows the effect of tube radius on the height to which capillary action can raise a fluid. (a) Calculate the height $\kh$ for water in a glass tube with a radius of 0.900 cm—a rather large tube like the one on the left. (b) What is the radius of the glass tube on the right if it raises water to 4.00 cm?

parts.hint: Water on glass has a contact angle of 0°, so $\cos\theta = 1$ in $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$; take the surface tension of water at 20°C from Table 11.3.
Solve the same equation for $r$ with $\kh = 4.00$ cm.

exercises.prompt: What fluid is in the device shown in Figure 11.26 if the force is $3.16\times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$ and the length of the wire is 2.50 cm? Calculate the surface tension $\kgamma$ and find a likely match from Table 11.3.

answer.hint: The film has two surfaces attached to the wire, so the length in $\kgamma = \kF/L$ is twice the length of the wire, $L = 2l$.
answer.solution: $6.32\times 10^{-2}\ \text{N/m}$. Based on the values in table, the fluid is probably glycerin.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the gauge pressures inside 2.00-cm-radius bubbles of water, alcohol, and soapy water. Which liquid forms the most stable bubbles, neglecting any effects of evaporation?

parts.hint: Use $\kPr = 4\kgamma/r$ with the surface tension of water at 20°C from Table 11.3 and the radius in meters.
The same equation with the surface tension of ethyl alcohol.
The same equation with the surface tension of soapy water.

answer.solution: $P_{\text{w}} = 14.6\ \text{N/m}^2$, $P_{\text{a}} = 4.46\ \text{N/m}^2$, $P_{\text{sw}} = 7.40\ \text{N/m}^2$. Alcohol forms the most stable bubble, since the absolute pressure inside is closest to atmospheric pressure.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the contact angle $\theta$ for olive oil if capillary action raises it to a height of 7.07 cm in a glass tube with a radius of 0.100 mm. Is this value consistent with that for most organic liquids?

answer.hint: Solve $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$ for $\cos\theta$, with the surface tension of olive oil from Table 11.3 and its density from Table 11.1.
answer.solution: $5.1^\circ$. This is near the value of $\theta = 0^\circ$ for most organic liquids.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the ratio of the heights to which water and mercury are raised by capillary action in the same glass tube.

answer.hint: Write $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$ for each liquid and divide; the radius and $\kg$ cancel, leaving the surface tensions from Table 11.3, the densities from Table 11.1 and the contact angles from Table 11.4.
answer.solution: $-2.78$. The ratio is negative because water is raised whereas mercury is lowered.

exercises.prompt: (a) How high will water rise in a glass capillary tube with a 0.500-mm radius? (b) How much gravitational potential energy does the water gain? (c) Discuss possible sources of this energy.

parts.hint: Water on glass has a contact angle of 0°; use $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$ with the surface tension of water at 20°C.
The column raised has a mass of $\krho\pi r^2\kh$, and its center of mass is raised by $\kh/2$.

answer.solution: (a) 2.97 cm (b) $3.39\times 10^{-6}\ \text{J}$ (c) Work is done by the surface tension force through an effective distance $\kh/2$ to raise the column of water.
